stem.text: A curve is defined by \( \left(y + 5\right)^{2} = \left(x + 6\right)^{2}\left(x + 18\right) \), and its derivative is \( \frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{\left(x + 6\right)\left(3x + 42\right)}{2\left(y + 5\right)} \). Find every point of the curve at which the tangent line is horizontal, or show that there is none.

answer_key.label: The tangent line is horizontal at \( (-14, 11) \) and \( (-14, -21) \).

worked_solution.text: A horizontal tangent needs the numerator of dy/dx to be 0 and the denominator to be nonzero. The numerator is 0 when \( x = -6 \) or \( x = -14 \).
worked_solution.rule_named: numerator of dy/dx equal to zero

worked_solution.text: On the curve, \( x = -6 \) forces \( y = -5 \), where the denominator is also 0, so \( (-6, -5) \) is not a point with a horizontal tangent.
Substituting \( x = -14 \) into the curve gives \( \left(y + 5\right)^{2} = 256 \), so \( y = 11 \) or \( y = -21 \), and the denominator is nonzero at both points.

options.label: The tangent line is horizontal at \( (-6, -5) \) and \( (-18, -5) \).
options.derivation: the denominator set to 0 instead of the numerator, which finds the points where y = v

options.label: The tangent line is horizontal at \( (-6, -5) \), \( (-14, 11) \) and \( (-14, -21) \).
options.derivation: the point (-6, -5), where the numerator is 0, kept without checking that the denominator is also 0 there

options.label: The tangent line is horizontal at \( (-14, 11) \) and \( (-14, -21) \).
The tangent line is horizontal at \( (-6, -5) \) and \( (-14, -5) \).
options.derivation: the numerator's roots paired with y = -5 and reported without substituting into the curve
